indicator.name: CoinMarketCap Crypto Market Metrics
indicator.description: A market-wide daily snapshot from CoinMarketCap containing aggregate cryptocurrency market capitalization, trading volume, market-share measures, sector-level market capitalization and volume, derivatives activity, market growth rates, and ecosystem activity statistics. The dataset provides a broad view of crypto-market size, liquidity, market structure, capital distribution, and changes in market activity within a single observation.
indicator.use: Monitor the overall size, liquidity, composition, activity, and structural changes of the cryptocurrency market using CoinMarketCap's aggregate market metrics.
indicator.purpose: Provide a consolidated market-wide snapshot for understanding total crypto-market capitalization, trading activity, Bitcoin and Ethereum market share, altcoin and DeFi market size, stablecoin liquidity, derivatives activity, and changes in the broader crypto ecosystem.
indicator.significance: CoinMarketCap Crypto Market Metrics provides broad market context that can be used to interpret changes across individual crypto assets and specialized indicators. Total market capitalization measures the aggregate value of the cryptocurrency market, while 24-hour spot trading volume provides a measure of market activity and liquidity. Altcoin market capitalization and volume help isolate activity outside Bitcoin, while Bitcoin and Ethereum dominance measure their respective shares of the total cryptocurrency market and can provide context for capital distribution and rotation. DeFi market capitalization and volume provide visibility into decentralized-finance activity, while stablecoin market capitalization and volume provide context for the size and activity of crypto-native liquidity instruments. Derivatives volume provides a measure of activity in crypto derivatives markets. The dataset also includes daily percentage changes in total market capitalization, total volume, DeFi activity, stablecoin activity, and derivatives activity, allowing the system to identify rapid changes in market conditions. Active cryptocurrency, market-pair, and exchange counts provide additional context for the size and breadth of the crypto ecosystem. These metrics can be analyzed alongside asset prices, market breadth, volatility, derivatives positioning, funding rates, stablecoin indicators, Bitcoin dominance, DeFi indicators, and macroeconomic conditions to identify changes in liquidity, market participation, capital rotation, and broader crypto-market regimes.

indicator.name: Alternative.me Crypto Fear & Greed Index
indicator.description: A daily composite index from Alternative.me measuring crypto-market sentiment on a scale from 0 to 100, where lower values represent greater fear and higher values represent greater greed. Alternative.me derives the index from multiple sentiment-related inputs, including Bitcoin volatility, market momentum and volume, social media activity, surveys, Bitcoin dominance, and Google Trends. Alternative.me's published methodology currently identifies the index as Bitcoin-focused.
indicator.use: Track daily changes in aggregate crypto-market sentiment using Alternative.me's composite Fear & Greed Index and its fear-to-greed classification.
indicator.purpose: Provide a standardized daily measure of market sentiment that can be used to identify shifts between fear, neutrality, and greed in the crypto market.
indicator.significance: The Alternative.me Crypto Fear & Greed Index combines multiple market and sentiment signals into a single 0-to-100 measure. Alternative.me's published methodology assigns 25% weight to volatility, 25% to market momentum and volume, 15% to social media, 15% to surveys, 10% to Bitcoin dominance, and 10% to Google Trends, although Alternative.me currently states that its surveys are paused. The index therefore captures several dimensions of market behavior rather than directly measuring investor sentiment through a single survey. It can be analyzed alongside price trends, volatility, trading volume, derivatives positioning, funding rates, market breadth, Bitcoin dominance, and other sentiment indicators to provide broader context for changes in crypto-market conditions.

indicator.name: CoinMarketCap Altcoin Season Index
indicator.description: A daily CoinMarketCap index measuring the relative performance of major altcoins versus Bitcoin over a rolling 90-day period. The index uses the top 100 eligible coins ranked on CoinMarketCap, excluding stablecoins and wrapped or asset-backed tokens, and scales the proportion of coins outperforming Bitcoin to a 0-to-100 index.
indicator.use: Track the degree to which major altcoins are outperforming or underperforming Bitcoin over a rolling 90-day period and identify shifts between Bitcoin-dominant and altcoin-dominant market regimes.
indicator.purpose: Provide a standardized measure of altcoin market breadth relative to Bitcoin and identify broad changes in relative performance across the cryptocurrency market.
indicator.significance: The CoinMarketCap Altcoin Season Index measures market breadth by comparing the rolling 90-day performance of the top 100 eligible coins on CoinMarketCap against Bitcoin. Stablecoins and wrapped or asset-backed tokens are excluded from the constituent set. The index reflects the proportion of these coins outperforming Bitcoin and is scaled from 1 to 100. Values above 75 indicate Altcoin Season, while values at or below 25 indicate Bitcoin Season. The index therefore measures the breadth of altcoin outperformance rather than sentiment directly: a high value means a large share of major altcoins have outperformed Bitcoin over the measurement period, while a low value means relatively few have done so. It can be analyzed alongside Bitcoin dominance, altcoin market capitalization, market breadth, liquidity, trading volume, and crypto-market sentiment to provide context for changes in market regime and capital rotation.

indicator.name: Bitcoin Spot ETF Market
indicator.description: A daily measure of U.S. spot Bitcoin ETF market activity, including aggregate net capital flows, traded value, net assets, and cumulative net flows. The indicator provides a view of capital entering or leaving the Bitcoin spot ETF market and the size and activity of the investment vehicles providing regulated market access to Bitcoin.
indicator.use: Track daily capital flows, trading activity, assets under management, and cumulative capital flows in the U.S. spot Bitcoin ETF market.
indicator.purpose: Provide a daily view of institutional and traditional-finance market participation in Bitcoin through regulated spot ETF vehicles and identify changes in capital allocation toward Bitcoin.
indicator.significance: Bitcoin spot ETF market data provides a direct view of capital flows and asset levels within regulated investment vehicles that give traditional investors access to Bitcoin. Net flow measures the daily net movement of capital into or out of the ETF market, while value traded measures ETF trading activity. Net assets indicate the aggregate size of assets held through the ETF vehicles, and cumulative net flow tracks the longer-term accumulation of capital flows since the measurement period began. Bitcoin ETF activity can provide important context for institutional and traditional-finance participation in Bitcoin and can be analyzed alongside Bitcoin price, Bitcoin dominance, derivatives positioning, open interest, funding rates, macroeconomic conditions, inflation expectations, interest rates, Treasury yields, liquidity conditions, and broader crypto-market sentiment. ETF flows should be interpreted as activity within the spot Bitcoin ETF market and should not be treated as a complete measure of all institutional Bitcoin ownership or total Bitcoin demand.

indicator.use: Track changes in Bitcoin futures open interest and positioning across dealers, asset managers, leveraged funds, other reportable traders, and nonreportable traders, including shifts in long, short, spreading, and net exposure.
indicator.purpose: Provide asset-specific visibility into how different classes of market participants are positioned in Bitcoin futures and how their exposure changes over time.

Changes in open interest reveal changes in futures-market participation, while changes in long and short positions show how each trader group is adjusting directional exposure. Separating trader classifications allows the intelligence system to distinguish institutional and leveraged positioning from dealer activity and aggregate nonreportable participation when analyzing Bitcoin market structure and sentiment.

indicator.purpose: Provide a core measure of short-term U.S. interest rates for monetary policy analysis, financial condition analysis, and cross-indicator interpretation within the intelligence system.
indicator.significance: The federal funds rate is a central short-term interest rate in the U.S. financial system. Changes in the rate influence other short-term rates and indirectly affect borrowing costs, financial conditions, economic activity, and asset markets.

indicator.name: 2-Year Treasury Yield
indicator.description: The market yield on U.S. Treasury securities with a constant maturity of two years, quoted on an investment basis. It reflects market expectations and pricing for short-term U.S. government borrowing.
indicator.use: Monitor short-term U.S. interest rates, Treasury market conditions, monetary policy expectations, and changes in the cost of government borrowing.
indicator.purpose: Provide a market-based measure of the two-year point on the U.S. Treasury yield curve for analyzing interest-rate expectations, monetary policy, financial conditions, and relationships across the yield curve.
indicator.significance: The two-year Treasury yield is closely connected to expectations for future monetary policy and short-term interest rates. Changes in the yield can provide information about shifts in interest-rate expectations and broader financial conditions.

indicator.name: 10-Year Treasury Yield
indicator.description: The market yield on U.S. Treasury securities with a constant maturity of ten years, quoted on an investment basis. It reflects market pricing for longer-term U.S. government borrowing and expectations about future economic and financial conditions.
indicator.use: Monitor long-term U.S. interest rates, Treasury market conditions, financial conditions, inflation and growth expectations, and changes in the cost of government borrowing.
indicator.purpose: Provide a market-based measure of the ten-year point on the U.S. Treasury yield curve for analyzing long-term interest rates, economic expectations, monetary policy transmission, and financial market conditions.
indicator.significance: The 10-year Treasury yield is a major benchmark for U.S. long-term interest rates and influences pricing across financial markets. Changes in the yield can reflect shifts in expectations for inflation, economic growth, monetary policy, and demand for government securities.

indicator.name: Real 10-Year Treasury Yield
indicator.description: The market yield on 10-year U.S. Treasury securities whose principal and interest payments are adjusted for inflation. It represents a market-based measure of the real interest rate for a 10-year maturity.
indicator.use: Monitor real long-term interest rates and assess changes in inflation-adjusted borrowing costs, financial conditions, and market expectations.
indicator.purpose: Provide a market-based measure of the real 10-year U.S. interest rate for analyzing real borrowing costs, inflation-adjusted returns, monetary policy, and financial conditions.
indicator.significance: The real 10-year Treasury yield provides information about the inflation-adjusted cost of long-term capital and the pricing of inflation-indexed government securities. Changes in the yield can affect financial conditions and the relative attractiveness of real versus nominal assets.

indicator.name: M2 Money Supply
indicator.description: A broad measure of the U.S. money supply consisting of currency and deposits and other liquid assets included in the Federal Reserve's M2 monetary aggregate. The series is seasonally adjusted and reported in billions of dollars.
indicator.use: Monitor changes in the quantity of money circulating through the U.S. financial system and assess changes in liquidity and monetary conditions.
indicator.purpose: Provide a broad measure of the U.S. money supply for analyzing monetary conditions, liquidity, financial activity, and relationships between money growth and broader economic conditions.
indicator.significance: M2 provides a broad measure of money and liquid deposits available within the U.S. financial system. Changes in M2 can provide information about shifts in monetary and liquidity conditions and can be analyzed alongside inflation, interest rates, credit, and economic activity.

indicator.name: Reverse Repo Usage
indicator.description: The aggregated daily amount of overnight reverse repurchase agreement transactions conducted by the Federal Reserve with eligible counterparties. The series is not seasonally adjusted and is reported in billions of U.S. dollars.
indicator.use: Monitor usage of the Federal Reserve's overnight reverse repurchase facility and assess changes in short-term liquidity and money-market conditions.
indicator.purpose: Provide a measure of overnight reverse repo activity for analyzing Federal Reserve open-market operations, money-market liquidity, reserve conditions, and changes in short-term financial conditions.
indicator.significance: Reverse repo usage reflects the amount of funds placed into the Federal Reserve's overnight reverse repurchase facility by eligible counterparties. Changes in usage can provide information about money-market conditions, the distribution of liquidity, and the interaction between Federal Reserve operations and short-term interest rates.

indicator.name: Nominal Broad U.S. Dollar Index
indicator.description: A trade-weighted index measuring the value of the U.S. dollar against a broad group of foreign currencies. The index is reported daily, is not seasonally adjusted, and uses January 2006 = 100 as its reference period.
indicator.use: Monitor changes in the broad nominal value of the U.S. dollar and assess foreign-exchange conditions, international financial conditions, trade competitiveness, and cross-border capital flows.
indicator.purpose: Provide a broad measure of U.S. dollar strength against major trading-partner currencies for analyzing foreign-exchange conditions, monetary policy transmission, global financial conditions, and relationships between the dollar and other asset markets.
indicator.significance: The broad U.S. dollar index provides a trade-weighted measure of changes in the dollar's value across a broad set of foreign currencies. Changes in the index can affect import prices, export competitiveness, international capital flows, commodity pricing, and global financial conditions.

indicator.name: Nominal Advanced Foreign Economies U.S. Dollar Index
indicator.description: A trade-weighted index measuring the nominal value of the U.S. dollar against currencies of advanced foreign economies. The index is reported daily, is not seasonally adjusted, and uses January 2006 = 100 as its reference period.
indicator.use: Monitor changes in the U.S. dollar's nominal value against currencies of advanced foreign economies and assess exchange-rate conditions, international financial conditions, and cross-border economic relationships.
indicator.purpose: Provide a trade-weighted measure of the U.S. dollar against advanced-economy currencies for analyzing foreign-exchange conditions, relative currency movements, monetary policy transmission, and international financial conditions.
indicator.significance: The index isolates movements in the U.S. dollar relative to currencies of advanced foreign economies using trade-weighted exchange rates. Changes can provide information about dollar strength, international capital conditions, trade relationships, and differences in monetary and economic conditions across major advanced economies.

indicator.name: Consumer Price Index
indicator.description: A seasonally adjusted price index measuring changes in the prices paid by urban consumers for a broad basket of goods and services in the United States. The index is based on a reference period of 1982–1984 = 100.
indicator.use: Monitor changes in consumer prices and assess inflation and deflation across the broad basket of goods and services purchased by urban consumers.
indicator.purpose: Provide a broad measure of changes in consumer prices for analyzing inflation trends, purchasing power, monetary policy, and economic conditions.
indicator.significance: The CPI is one of the primary measures used to monitor consumer price changes in the U.S. Changes in the index can indicate shifts in inflationary or deflationary conditions and are relevant to monetary policy, household purchasing power, and economic analysis.

indicator.name: Personal Consumption Expenditures
indicator.description: A measure of spending by households on goods and services in the United States. The series is reported as a seasonally adjusted annual rate and expressed in billions of dollars.
indicator.use: Monitor household consumption and changes in consumer spending, a major component of U.S. economic activity.
indicator.purpose: Provide a broad measure of personal consumption expenditures for analyzing consumer demand, economic growth, household spending behavior, and broader economic conditions.
indicator.significance: Personal consumption expenditures represent a major component of U.S. economic activity. Changes in consumer spending can provide information about household demand, economic momentum, and shifts in consumption patterns.

indicator.name: Nonfarm Payrolls
indicator.description: The number of employees in the U.S. nonfarm economy, excluding proprietors, private household employees, unpaid volunteers, farm employees, and the unincorporated self-employed. The series is seasonally adjusted and reported in thousands of persons.
indicator.use: Monitor changes in total nonfarm employment and assess labor-market conditions, job creation, and changes in overall economic activity.
indicator.purpose: Provide a broad measure of U.S. employment for analyzing labor-market strength, economic growth, household income, business activity, and changes in the business cycle.
indicator.significance: Nonfarm payrolls are a major measure of U.S. employment and provide information about changes in the number of jobs across the economy. Sustained increases or decreases can provide insight into labor-market conditions and broader economic momentum.

indicator.name: Unemployment Rate
indicator.description: The percentage of the U.S. civilian labor force that is unemployed. This series represents the U-3 measure of labor underutilization and is seasonally adjusted.
indicator.use: Monitor labor market conditions and changes in the share of the labor force that is unemployed.
indicator.purpose: Provide a core measure of U.S. labor market conditions for analyzing employment, economic activity, monetary policy, household conditions, and changes in the business cycle.
indicator.significance: The unemployment rate is a widely used measure of labor market conditions and economic slack. Changes in unemployment can provide information about labor-market strength, household income conditions, economic activity, and the broader business cycle.

indicator.name: CNN Fear & Greed Index
indicator.description: A daily composite index designed by CNN to measure prevailing fear and greed in the U.S. stock market using multiple market-behavior indicators. The index ranges from 0 to 100, with lower values representing greater fear and higher values representing greater greed.
indicator.use: Monitor changes in U.S. equity-market sentiment, investor risk appetite, market momentum, volatility, and demand for defensive assets, and identify shifts between risk-seeking and risk-averse market conditions.
indicator.purpose: Provide a compact market-sentiment signal that summarizes several observable characteristics of U.S. equity markets into a single daily measure for tracking changes in investor risk appetite and market stress.
indicator.significance: The Fear & Greed Index provides a behavioral measure of the prevailing emotional conditions in U.S. equity markets. Changes in the index can indicate shifts in market momentum, volatility, demand for safe-haven assets, and willingness to take risk. It can therefore provide context for interpreting market moves alongside prices, volatility measures, credit conditions, and broader financial-market indicators.

indicator.name: CNN Market Volatility (VIX vs 50-Day Moving Average)
indicator.description: A daily market-volatility indicator based on the CBOE Volatility Index (VIX) relative to its 50-day moving average. The VIX reflects expected S&P 500 volatility over the following 30 days, while its relationship with the 50-day average is used by CNN as a measure of changing market volatility and fear.
indicator.use: Monitor changes in expected U.S. equity-market volatility and identify shifts in market stress, risk aversion, and investor sentiment through the VIX's relationship with its 50-day trend.
indicator.purpose: Provide a volatility-based measure of U.S. equity-market conditions that captures whether expected market volatility is increasing or decreasing relative to its recent trend.
indicator.significance: The VIX provides a forward-looking measure of expected S&P 500 volatility derived from options prices. Comparing it with its 50-day moving average adds a trend dimension that helps identify changes in market stress and risk perception. Rising volatility relative to its trend is interpreted by CNN as a signal of fear, while declining volatility is associated with greed. As one component of the Fear & Greed framework, it complements momentum, breadth, options positioning, and other measures of market behavior.

indicator.name: CNN Safe Haven Demand
indicator.description: A daily measure of the difference between U.S. Treasury bond and stock returns over the previous 20 trading days. It is used by CNN to assess whether investors are favoring safer Treasury assets over riskier equities.
indicator.use: Monitor shifts between equity risk-taking and demand for safer Treasury assets, and identify changes in investor risk appetite, defensive positioning, and market stress.
indicator.purpose: Provide a cross-asset measure of investor risk preference by comparing recent stock and Treasury performance over a 20-trading-day period.
indicator.significance: Safe Haven Demand captures changes in investor preference between riskier equities and safer Treasury assets. When Treasury bonds outperform stocks, it can indicate increased demand for defensive assets and greater risk aversion; when stocks outperform Treasuries, it indicates stronger relative demand for risk assets. As a component of CNN's Fear & Greed framework, it adds a cross-asset risk-preference signal that complements equity momentum, breadth, volatility, and options positioning.

indicator.name: AAII Investor Sentiment Survey
indicator.description: A weekly survey of individual investors measuring the percentage who expect the U.S. stock market to rise, remain essentially unchanged, or fall over the next six months. The dataset includes bullish, neutral, bearish, and bull-bear spread readings.
indicator.use: Monitor changes in individual-investor expectations, optimism, pessimism, uncertainty, and overall sentiment toward the U.S. stock market, including changes in the bull-bear spread.
indicator.purpose: Provide a direct survey-based measure of individual-investor expectations that complements market-derived sentiment indicators by capturing what retail investors expect the stock market to do over the following six months.
indicator.significance: The AAII Sentiment Survey provides a direct measure of individual-investor expectations rather than inferring sentiment from market prices or positioning. Changes in bullish, neutral, and bearish responses reveal shifts in optimism, pessimism, and uncertainty, while the bull-bear spread summarizes the balance between optimistic and pessimistic views. Extreme sentiment readings can provide useful context for assessing investor psychology and potential sentiment reversals, but the survey does not establish the future direction of the market.

indicator.name: IG Gold Retail Positioning
indicator.description: A daily measure of long and short positioning among retail traders on the IG trading platform for gold. The indicator reports the percentage of IG retail traders holding long and short positions and the resulting net positioning. This data represents IG's own retail trader pool and is not a market-wide measure of all retail traders or investors.
indicator.use: Track daily changes in long and short positioning among IG retail traders exposed to gold, including the distribution of positions and the resulting net retail positioning.
indicator.purpose: Provide a daily view of how IG's retail trader population is positioned toward gold and how that positioning changes over time.
indicator.significance: IG gold retail positioning provides a daily view of directional exposure among retail traders using the IG trading platform. The indicator can provide context for retail sentiment, speculative positioning, and changes in exposure to gold. Because the dataset represents only IG's retail trader pool rather than the entire retail-investor population, it should be interpreted as a broker-specific positioning signal rather than a comprehensive measure of overall retail sentiment. Gold positioning can be analyzed alongside gold prices, safe-haven demand, inflation expectations, real interest rates, Treasury yields, the U.S. dollar, Federal Reserve policy, and broader financial-market conditions to provide additional context for changes in gold-market positioning.

items.headline: One year after crypto's $20 billion liquidation day, the lesson for Bitcoin traders
items.summary: A year ago this weekend, crypto markets went through the largest forced-selling event in their history. Bitcoin set a record high of $126,080 on 6 October 2025. Four days later, a sudden escalation in US-China trade tensions triggered a wave of liquidations that wiped out roughly $20 billion in leveraged positions over a single weekend. A year on, Bitcoin trades roughly a third below that peak. The anniversary is worth marking for two reasons. First, the mechanics that turned a political headline into a market rout are still in place today. Second, October's reputation as a strong month for Bitcoin can make traders careless at exactly the wrong moment. What happened in October 2025 On Friday 10 October (US time), President Donald Trump announced 100% tariffs on Chinese imports, effective 1 November. Risk assets sold off. Crypto trades around the clock and carries heavy leverage, so it took the hardest hit. Bitcoin fell as much as 15%, dropping towards $100,000 on some exchanges. Ether fell more than 20%. Some smaller tokens briefly traded at or near zero on certain venues. When US markets reopened on Monday, spot Bitcoin and Ether ETFs recorded combined outflows of more than $755 million. What a liquidation actually is Many crypto traders use leverage, which means borrowing to take a bigger position than their own cash would allow. The trader puts up collateral, called margin. If the price moves far enough against the position that the margin can no longer cover the losses, the exchange closes the position automatically. That forced close is a liquidation. At 10 times leverage, a move of roughly 10% against the trade is enough to wipe out the margin (fees can make it happen sooner). At 25 times leverage, a move of about 4% is enough. When a leveraged long position is liquidated, the exchange sells into the market. That selling pushes the price lower, which triggers the next layer of liquidations, which pushes the price lower again. This chain reaction is called a liquidation cascade. Thin weekend trading makes it worse, because fewer buyers are available to absorb the forced selling. The key point is that the size of the October 2025 drop was not only about the tariff news. It was about how much leverage had built up in the market, waiting for a trigger. Why one green October proves nothing Bitcoin's October record helps explain why traders were so comfortable going into last year's crash. Bitcoin has closed October higher in 10 of the past 13 years, with a median gain of about 15%. That track record gave the month its "Uptober" nickname. October 2025 shows the limits of that record. Bitcoin made a new all-time high early in the month, crashed four days later, and still finished October down 3.7%. Seasonal patterns describe what has happened before. They do not cause anything to happen. Thirteen years is a small sample, and a single shock can outweigh a pattern built over a decade. This October has started reasonably well. According to CryptoQuant data, Bitcoin closed 3 October up 1.4% from its September close. That is a decent start, but it is not evidence of how the month will end. What could matter more than the calendar this month Macro conditions look more important than seasonality this October. The Federal Reserve meets on 27 and 28 October. Rate hikes remain a live possibility: in June, half of Fed officials projected at least one hike in 2026. Bitfinex has argued that the main constraint on Bitcoin right now is the return available on low-risk assets, not sentiment towards crypto. If real yields keep rising, Bitcoin has to work harder to attract buyers, whatever the calendar says. What to watch next Open interest versus price. Open interest is the total value of open futures positions. If it keeps rising while the price goes nowhere, leverage is building, and that is the kind of setup that produced last year's cascade. Funding rates. Funding is the regular payment between long and short traders in perpetual futures. Persistently high positive funding suggests the market is crowded on the long side. The 28 October Fed decision, and the US data released before it. Weekend liquidity. Big moves on thin weekend volume are more likely to be driven by liquidations than by real buying or selling. What would change the interpretation? If Bitcoin breaks out of its current range while open interest stays flat or falls, the move is more likely being driven by spot buying than by borrowed money. That would be a healthier signal. For readers who use leverage, the practical lesson of October 2025 is about survival rather than direction. The question to ask is not whether October will be green. It is whether your positions could withstand a sudden 15% move on a quiet weekend. This article was written by Eamonn Sheridan at investinglive.com.

results.title: Wells Fargo in talks with Kraken parent Payward for crypto
highlights: Wells Fargo in talks with Kraken parent Payward for crypto trading liquidity The discussions would see Payward supply liquidity for crypto trading as major banks deepen their involvement in digital assets. - Payward is in talks to become a crypto liquidity provider to Wells Fargo, according to sources. - The potential deal would involve supplying liquidity for trading digital assets. - Wells Fargo previously advised Nasdaq on its $100 million investment in Payward. Payward, the parent company of crypto exchange Kraken, is in talks to become a crypto liquidity provider to U.S. financial giant Wells Fargo (WFC), according to two people with direct knowledge of the matter. Under the potential deal, Wyoming-based Payward would supply liquidity for trading in crypto assets, the people said, speaking on condition of anonymity because the matter is private. Talks are ongoing and may not result in a deal. Crypto exchanges often serve as gateways to digital asset liquidity for banks and institutional investors, providing access to trading venues and helping execute orders. For example, Coinbase Prime aggregates liquidity across multiple markets, while Kraken offers banks technology to integrate crypto trading into their own platforms, allowing them to serve clients without building the infrastructure themselves The discussions suggest major banks are increasingly turning to established crypto companies to support their digital asset ambitions. A friendlier U.S. regulatory environment is also helping drive that shift. Under a more accommodating regulatory climate during President Donald Trump’s administration, major lenders are increasingly viewing established digital asset companies such as Payward as commercial partners, signaling the sector’s growing acceptance within traditional finance. Wells Fargo already offers spot bitcoin exchange-traded funds (ETFs) to eligible wealth clients and has backed crypto compliance firm Elliptic and trading technology provider Talos. It has also announced plans for blockchain-based deposits and joined a consortium developing a dollar stablecoin, extending its digital asset activities into payments. The California-based financial services firm strengthened its digital assets team earlier this year by hiring former Citi (C) banker Mark Gracia. The bank also served as Nasdaq’s exclusive capital markets adviser on the exchange operator’s September agreement to invest $100 million in Payward and deepen their collaboration on tokenized equities and market surveillance.

results.title: $2.3T Wells Fargo in Talks With Kraken Parent Payward for
highlights: $2.3T Wells Fargo in Talks With Kraken Parent Payward for Crypto Trading Liquidity - Wells Fargo is in early talks with Payward, Kraken’s parent, to source crypto liquidity for its digital-asset trading, though no deal is confirmed. - Under the “rent the rails” model, Payward would route and price trades via Kraken Prime while Wells Fargo keeps its client relationships and brand. - The talks follow Payward’s growing bank network, with SoFi live, SGB Net integrated, and BNY also reported to be in broader discussions. Wells Fargo, the U.S. banking giant managing roughly $2.3 trillion in assets, is in talks with Payward, Kraken’s parent company, to supply crypto liquidity for the bank’s digital-asset trading operations. According to a report on October 7, the talks are ongoing and may not produce a deal. Both sides declined to comment publicly. The proposed arrangement is not a custody mandate or a balance-sheet Bitcoin purchase. Under the structure being discussed, Payward would act as an execution-layer crypto liquidity provider. Wells Fargo keeps its client relationships and brand intact. Payward, through Kraken Prime, its institutional prime brokerage arm, would handle the routing and pricing of digital-asset trades. In simple terms: Wells Fargo clients get the crypto trading experience; Payward powers the market behind it. That is the “rent the rails” model. It lets a megabank enter digital-asset trading at low capital cost, without running its own matching engine. A liquidity deal with Payward would extend that footprint from passive ETF exposure into active crypto trading rails. The relationship between the two firms is also not new. Wells Fargo served as Nasdaq’s exclusive capital-markets adviser when Nasdaq invested $100 million in in September , a deal that valued the exchange at $21 billion and deepened collaboration on tokenized equities and market surveillance. A liquidity deal would push that adjacency from advisory work into live commercial infrastructure. The Wells Fargo talks surface as Payward builds an accelerating stack of banking partnerships Earlier in October, Kraken’s parent integrated SGB Net, Singapore Gulf Bank’s real-time settlement network, so institutional clients on both platforms can settle digital-asset trades around the clock, starting with U.S. dollar transactions. Singapore Gulf Bank is also onboarding Kraken Prime as an extra liquidity source for its own clients. Separately, BNY, one of the world’s largest custodians, is reported to be in broader talks with Payward covering digital assets, custody, wealth, trading, and infrastructure. SoFi Technologies went live with a similar arrangement in early September, routing customer crypto liquidity through Kraken Prime and joining Payward’s settlement network for 24-hour-a-day dollar movement. Payward’s anticipated public listing, Scope, eligible clients, and asset classes covered by the Wells Fargo–Payward talks remain undisclosed. No product launch or 8-K disclosure has been filed. The arrangement would only be confirmed if both sides reach an agreement and choose to announce it publicly.

results.title: Kraken parent Payward in talks with BNY over crypto partnership - Finalcrux
highlights: Kraken parent Payward in talks with BNY over crypto partnership Payward, the parent company of crypto exchange Kraken, has entered talks with BNY about a potential partnership spanning six business lines, including crypto custody, trading and payments, according to Crypto.news. Two people familiar with the discussions, who spoke anonymously because the negotiations are private, said no agreement is guaranteed. Payward and BNY are discussing a potential partnership covering crypto products, custody, wealth management, trading, payments and financial infrastructure. The talks were first reported by Crypto.news on October 2, 2026, with PANews reporting the same discussions on October 3. Negotiations remain ongoing and no deal has been confirmed. The proposed arrangement could involve services supplied through Payward Services, the Wyoming-based company’s platform for banks, exchanges and asset managers, one of the people said. Parts of the discussions resemble the infrastructure work included in Payward’s recent agreement with Nasdaq. Key facts Payward and BNY are discussing six areas of potential cooperation: crypto products, custody, wealth management, trading, payments and financial infrastructure, per Crypto.news. Talks are ongoing with no guarantee of an agreement, according to people cited by both Crypto.news and PANews. Nasdaq Ventures agreed in September 2026 to invest $100 million in Payward at a reported $21 billion valuation, tied to tokenized equity infrastructure and a market surveillance arrangement. Payward closed its Bitnomial US derivatives acquisition on May 1, 2026, and its $600 million Reap stablecoin payments acquisition on July 1. BNY’s deposit-tokenization program, announced January 9, 2026, began with collateral and margin workflows on a private, permissioned blockchain. What both reports agree on, and where they diverge Crypto.news and PANews describe the same core story: two people familiar with the matter say BNY and Payward are negotiating a broad digital-asset and market-infrastructure partnership, with services delivered through Payward Services and an infrastructure component echoing the Nasdaq agreement. The two accounts differ in framing rather than substance. Crypto.news credits its own reporting and identifies BNY as formerly Bank of New York Mellon, a provider of custody, asset servicing, clearing and wealth management for institutional clients, listed on the NYSE under BK. PANews credits CoinDesk for the underlying report, describing BNY as a “custody banking giant” and calling the scope a “broad partnership” covering digital assets and financial market infrastructure. Neither report names the individuals involved, and PANews, like Crypto.news, notes there is no guarantee a deal will be reached. Why the BNY talks fit Payward’s recent dealmaking The reported discussions follow a stretch of consolidation for Payward. On the exchange side, the company is building out regulated US derivatives through its Bitnomial purchase, which brought a designated contract market, a derivatives clearing organization and a futures commission merchant under the CFTC’s framework. Payward said it would connect that infrastructure across Kraken, NinjaTrader and Payward Services, giving banks, brokerages and payment firms access to regulated US crypto derivatives through a single integration. Those moves sit alongside the Nasdaq arrangement, which Crypto.news reported on September 10 at a $21 billion valuation and which packages three components: the $100 million investment, further work on Nasdaq Equity Tokens, and a market surveillance agreement. Under that deal, Payward will adopt Nasdaq’s surveillance technology across crypto, equities, tokenized equities, futures and options venues, and the two expect to launch equity tokens in the second quarter of 2027. Nasdaq named Wells Fargo its exclusive capital markets adviser on the transaction. On the banking side, BNY has been building institutional digital-cash capabilities. Its January 9 announcement described creating blockchain records that mirror participating clients’ existing deposit balances, starting with collateral and margin workflows. The bank said the digital entries represent clients’ demand deposit claims against BNY, run on a private, permissioned blockchain, and continue to appear in its traditional records for regulatory and reporting purposes. Rules-based, near-real-time cash movement was identified as a future objective for institutional clients. Why it matters A tie-up between a crypto-native group and one of the largest custody banks would matter beyond the two firms. It would put regulated banking infrastructure and crypto trading, custody and payments capability under one commercial relationship, at a time when traditional custodians and exchanges are converging on tokenized assets and digital cash. For banks, brokers and asset managers weighing digital-asset exposure, it would also create a route through a single B2B provider rather than a patchwork of vendors. The talks follow a broader pattern in which crypto companies buy regulated US market infrastructure, while established banks build tokenized deposit rails rather than standalone crypto products. What to watch The next concrete checkpoint is whether Payward and BNY confirm an agreement, which neither has done so far. Separately, the Nasdaq-linked equity token launch, which the two companies said they expect in the second quarter of 2027, remains a measurable milestone for Payward’s tokenized market infrastructure work. What areas could a Payward-BNY partnership cover? Reports cite crypto products, custody, wealth management, trading, payments and financial infrastructure, with services potentially delivered through Payward Services, the company’s B2B platform for banks, exchanges and asset managers. Is a Payward-BNY deal confirmed? No. Both Crypto.news and PANews say the talks are ongoing and there is no guarantee the companies will reach an agreement.

Samsung paired the reveal with the launch of its first branded credit card, built with Barclays on the Visa network, tying a conventional financial product to a wallet the company now frames as a broader hub for digital assets. No issuer agreement, launch date or list of supported regions has been finalized, but the intent marks one of the largest hardware-based pushes stablecoins have received from a consumer electronics maker. Samsung has said only that Wallet’s financial features run under Samsung Knox, the security platform built into Galaxy devices, with end-to-end encryption protecting sensitive data. The company has not specified whether stablecoin balances will rely on Knox Vault, the tamper-resistant chip introduced with the Galaxy S21 in 2021, or on Samsung Blockchain Keystore, the hardware-backed key storage that debuted with the Galaxy S10 in 2019. Samsung does have a longer track record here than most phone makers, since Galaxy devices have shipped with hardware-protected crypto key storage since 2019. The bigger open question is custody. Samsung has not said whether users will hold their own keys on the device, whether balances will sit with an exchange partner like Coinbase, or whether an issuer such as Circle will manage them on the back end. Each model carries a different regulatory load, and the one Samsung picks will decide how much compliance work lands on the company itself once the feature ships. It is assembling infrastructure, regulatory positioning, and distribution into a single strategy that could reshape how stablecoins reach ordinary consumers, or could stall at the mockup stage if the missing pieces do not come together. The demo showed a wallet interface labeled USDC with three action buttons. A Samsung Wallet stablecoin feature in the United States would need to work with a GENIUS Act compliant issuer, a licensed custodian, and a blockchain settlement layer that meets the law’s requirements for reserve transparency and redemption rights. The law requires payment stablecoin issuers to maintain one to one reserves in high quality liquid assets such as United States Treasury securities, insured deposits, or central bank reserves. Issuers must also publish monthly attestations of reserve composition audited by a registered accounting firm. A Samsung implementation on one network would place that network on the default route offered through Wallet. On June 30, 2025, BitMine announced its transformation into an Ethereum treasury company, with the goal of buying 5% of the ETH supply.
